Past a handful of endpoints the default client is `dio`, because interceptors, cancellation, multipart and base-URL handling come built in.

### Choosing a client
- **http** — official, tiny, no interceptors; fine when you have a few calls and no auth refresh
- **dio** — interceptors, CancelToken, FormData, response transformers, per-request options

### Choosing a serialization approach
- **Hand-written fromJson/toJson** — no build step, fine for a few models, easy to get subtly wrong
- **json\_serializable** — code generation; a renamed field fails at build time instead of at runtime
- **freezed** — immutable models plus copyWith, ==, and unions; the usual production choice

### The call path, in order
1. Build the request — base URL, headers, query parameters
2. Send it and check the status code
3. Decode the body into a model, or map the failure into a typed domain error
4. Render loading, data or error from that single result

Keep `Map<String, dynamic>` out of the UI layer. Decode at the repository boundary so widgets only ever see models.

Infinite scroll is a paging cursor plus a scroll trigger that fires once, near the bottom of the list.

The list asks for the next page as the user approaches the end, and must refuse to ask twice while a request is in flight.

### Paging strategies
- **Offset** — `?page=2&limit=20`; simplest, but items shift or repeat if rows are inserted while the user scrolls
- **Cursor** — `?after=cursor123`; stable under concurrent writes, the usual choice for feeds
- **Keyset** — `?last_id=500`; cheapest on the database for very large tables

### On the Flutter side
- A ScrollController listener (or NotificationListener\<ScrollNotification>) to detect the bottom
- ListView.builder with one extra trailing item for the loading indicator
- **State to track**: items, isLoading, hasMore, error
- **Guard re-entrancy** — a scroll listener fires on every pixel, so bail out while a request is in flight
- infinite\_scroll\_pagination if you would rather not own the paging state machine

The bug interviewers look for: no isLoading guard, so one flick of the thumb fires the same page request five times.

An interceptor runs on every request, response and error, so cross-cutting concerns live in one place instead of at every call site.

### What they are used for
- Attaching auth headers to every request
- Logging requests and responses
- Mapping transport failures into typed domain errors
- Refreshing an expired token and replaying the original request
- Retrying on transient network errors

### How they work in Dio
- Add an `Interceptor` (or `InterceptorsWrapper`) to `dio.interceptors`
- `onRequest`, `onResponse`, `onError` each get a handler — call `handler.next(...)` to continue, `handler.resolve(response)` to short-circuit with success, `handler.reject(err)` to fail
- Interceptors run in the order they were added, so put logging last if you want to see the auth header
- The `http` package has no interceptor concept — you wrap `http.Client` in a subclass and override `send`

The trap in a refresh-token interceptor: retrying through the same Dio instance re-enters the interceptor, so a permanently invalid token loops forever. Guard with a flag on the request options, and funnel concurrent 401s into a single in-flight refresh.

File uploads use multipart/form-data, which packages each field — including binary file content — into a single request body. Both `http` and `dio` support it; Dio's API is more ergonomic.

### Key pieces
- **MultipartFile** — wraps a file (path, bytes, or stream) plus filename and contentType
- **FormData** — collection of fields and multipart files
- `Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=...` is set automatically; do NOT set it yourself or you'll break the boundary

### Sources for the file
- `image_picker` for camera/gallery on mobile
- `file_picker` for any file type, including web (where you only get bytes, not paths)
- Streamed uploads (large files) — use MultipartFile.fromStream + setting filename

### Progress
- Dio's `onSendProgress: (sent, total) {...}` fires throughout the upload — wire it to a progress indicator
- For long-running uploads, use a CancelToken and let the user cancel

### Server-side hooks
- Multipart sends fields as form parts named `field`, files as `file` (or whatever you choose); make sure the server's parser matches your field names
- For upload-then-confirm patterns (S3 presigned URLs), there is no multipart at all — you PUT the bytes directly to the signed URL with `Content-Type` matching what was signed

Caching cuts network traffic, makes repeat views feel instant, and buys you limited offline use. Three layers, each right for a different case.

### HTTP cache headers (server-driven)
- The server sends `Cache-Control: max-age=N` plus an `ETag` or `Last-Modified`
- The client sends `If-None-Match` next time and gets a 304 Not Modified if nothing changed
- Flutter has no browser cache to lean on — `dio_cache_interceptor` is the canonical package

### Application-level cache
- Store the parsed model in a local database (sqflite, drift, hive\_ce, ObjectBox)
- **Strategy**: stale-while-revalidate — return the cached value immediately, refresh in the background, swap in the fresh one
- Best when data has a natural expiry, or when you want offline-first behaviour

### Image cache
- `cached_network_image` adds a disk cache so images survive app restarts
- `precacheImage` decodes into memory before the user navigates

### Picking one
- REST GETs that change rarely — HTTP cache, or app-level stale-while-revalidate
- **Real-time data** — do not cache; subscribe to a stream instead
- **Authenticated responses** — private scope only, never shared between users

The failure mode to name in an interview is cache poisoning: caching 4xx/5xx responses, or keying a per-user response by URL alone so the next user reads it. Key by URL plus relevant query params plus the signed-in user.

WebSockets give you a long-lived bidirectional channel — push from server, send from client, no polling. The two parts that matter in production are: structuring the lifecycle and reconnecting on failure.

### Libraries
- `web_socket_channel` — the official lightweight client; simple Stream-based API
- `socket_io_client` — for Socket.IO servers (which are NOT plain WebSocket)

### Lifecycle
- `WebSocketChannel.connect(uri)` opens the connection
- `channel.stream` is a Stream of incoming events; subscribe and handle messages
- `channel.sink.add(message)` sends; `sink.close()` closes
- Treat the channel like a single-subscription stream — wrap in your own service if you need fan-out

### Reconnection
- **WebSockets DO break** — flaky networks, server restarts, idle proxies. Always plan for reconnect.
- **Pattern**: state machine `Disconnected → Connecting → Connected → Disconnected (with backoff)`
- Exponential backoff with jitter, capped (e.g., 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s, 30s, 60s)
- **Heartbeat / ping**: send a ping every 20–30s; if no pong in time, treat as disconnect
- **Resume gracefully**: server should send last-seen sequence numbers so client can request missed events

### App lifecycle
- On `AppLifecycleState.paused` (Android backgrounding, iOS app switcher): close cleanly
- On `resumed`: reconnect from scratch
- Otherwise the OS may kill your socket without notice and you'll send into a broken pipe

### Authentication
- Pass token in the connection URL (`wss://api.example.com/socket?token=...`) or first message
- **On token refresh, reconnect** — there's no "in-flight rotate" for ws auth

Catching `DioException` everywhere bleeds the HTTP layer into your business logic. The clean pattern: a single error mapper translates Dio failures into a typed hierarchy your repositories and view models can handle without knowing about HTTP at all.

DioException.type variants:
- `connectionTimeout` — TCP/TLS handshake didn't complete in time
- `sendTimeout` / `receiveTimeout` — slow upload/download
- `badResponse` — server returned 4xx/5xx; check `error.response?.statusCode`
- `cancel` — your code cancelled via CancelToken
- `connectionError` — DNS, network down, no route
- `badCertificate` — TLS validation failure
- `unknown` — anything else; usually wraps another exception in `error.error`

### Typical domain hierarchy
- `NetworkException` — connectivity / timeout / unknown
- `ServerException(int statusCode, String? message)` — 5xx
- `BadRequestException(message, fields)` — 4xx with structured payload
- `UnauthorizedException` — 401, often triggers a refresh-token flow
- `ForbiddenException` — 403, no retry
- `NotFoundException` — 404
- `ConflictException` — 409 / unique-key violation
- `Cancelled` — user-initiated

### Where to map
- In a Dio interceptor's `onError` — keep the entry point clean
- OR in a single helper called from each repository method (`api.runOrThrow(() => dio.get(...))`)
- Either way, callers see only domain exceptions

Offline-first means the app works without a network and syncs in the background. The user never waits for the network on a write — local changes are applied immediately, then reconciled.

Building blocks:

1. Local source of truth — a real database (sqflite, drift, isar). The UI reads from it.
2. Mutation queue — every write (create/update/delete) is journaled to a `pending_ops` table with a unique id and idempotency key.
3. Apply locally first — the write also updates the main tables, marking the row as `dirty` (or `synced=false`).
4. Sync engine — a background worker that drains the queue: sends each pending op to the server, receives the canonical version, and reconciles.
5. Pull updates — periodically (or via WebSocket / push), fetch server changes since a `cursor`/`updated_at` and apply them locally.
6. Conflict resolution — last-write-wins is simple but loses data; field-level merge (CRDTs / OT / version vectors) is correct but complex. Pick based on data sensitivity.

### Rules
- Every mutation must have an idempotency key. The server uses it to dedupe — if the client retries after a crash, the server doesn't double-apply.
- The UI never reads from the network directly. It only reads from the local DB. The network feeds the local DB.
- When sync fails for non-retryable reasons (4xx), surface to the user and stop retrying.
- Use connectivity\_plus to know when to wake the sync engine.

### Gotchas
- Do not store arbitrary Future\<void> in the queue — store data: `op_type`, `payload`, `idempotency_key`. Reconstruct the request from data on each retry.
- Order matters for related writes (create user → create user's first note). Persist a per-aggregate sequence number.
- Schema changes between client versions need a queue migration, not just a schema migration.

GraphQL is a single endpoint where the client describes the data it wants in a typed query language. The server returns exactly that — no over-fetching, no under-fetching. It pairs well with Flutter when:

- You have a backend that already speaks GraphQL (Apollo / Hasura / Hot Chocolate / your own)
- Different screens need different shapes of data (deep, nested) and you'd otherwise create a sprawl of REST endpoints
- You want a strongly-typed client without writing fromJson by hand

Main library: `graphql_flutter` (built on `graphql` \+ `gql`). It ships:
- HttpLink + AuthLink + WebSocketLink for transport
- Cache-first / network-first / cache-and-network policies
- Query, Mutation, Subscription widgets
- Code-gen via `graphql_codegen` (or `ferry` ecosystem) for type-safe operations

### When NOT to use
- Your backend is a plain REST CRUD; adding GraphQL doesn't pay for itself
- Tiny app with two endpoints — REST is simpler
- **File uploads** — possible, but REST/multipart is more straightforward

### Gotchas
- **Cache normalization** — graphql\_flutter normalizes by `__typename` \+ `id`. Without `id` in your queries, cache updates are messy.
- **Pagination** — Relay-style `connection { edges { node { id } } pageInfo }` is the conventional shape; design your queries around it from day one.
- Subscriptions need a WebSocket transport (`WebSocketLink`); reconnection and auth come with the same caveats as plain WebSockets.

Give the screen its own CancelToken, pass it to every request the screen starts, and cancel it from dispose.

### With Dio
- Create one `CancelToken` per screen or per logical operation, pass it as `cancelToken:` to each call, and call `token.cancel('screen closed')` in `dispose()`.
- The pending Future completes with a `DioException` whose type is `cancel`. Treat that as a normal outcome — never show it as an error to the user.
- A cancelled token stays cancelled. For the next request, create a new one; reusing it fails immediately.
- For search-as-you-type, cancel the previous token before starting the next request so only the newest one can win.

### With package:http
- There is no token. Hold an `http.Client`, and call `client.close()` to abort what it has in flight, then build a new client for later work.

### Around the call site
- Cancel the StreamSubscription too if you consumed a streamed response.
- Check `mounted` (or a `_disposed` flag in a notifier) after every await before touching state or context.
- In a bloc, a `restartable()` transformer cancels the previous handler for you; in Riverpod, `ref.onDispose(token.cancel)` on an autoDispose provider does the same job.

One caveat worth saying out loud: cancelling is a client-side act. The request may already have reached the server and may still be applied, so for writes rely on idempotency keys instead of assuming a cancelled call did nothing.

Stream the response straight to a temporary file, report progress from the received-bytes callback, and resume by asking the server for the remaining byte range.

### Progress
- `dio.download(url, tempPath, onReceiveProgress: (received, total) {...})` gives you both numbers. `total` is -1 when the server sends no Content-Length, so show an indeterminate bar in that case.
- Throttle UI updates. Rebuilding on every chunk costs more than the download itself; update a ValueNotifier a few times a second.

### Resuming
- Send `Range: bytes=<downloaded>-` and append to the partial file. A server that supports it answers 206 Partial Content and advertises `Accept-Ranges: bytes`.
- If it answers 200 instead, the range was ignored — truncate the partial file and start over.
- Store the partial file plus its expected size and ETag. If the ETag changed, the file on the server is a different one; discard and restart.

### Correctness details that matter in production
- Download to `<name>.part` in the temporary or cache directory and rename it into place only after the last byte arrives. A crash then never leaves a half file that looks complete.
- **Verify what you got** — compare the final size with Content-Length, or a checksum if the API provides one.
- Check free space before starting, and delete partial files on cleanup.
- Pass a CancelToken so the user can stop it, and keep the file for a later resume.
- A Dart download stops when the OS suspends or kills the app. For downloads that must survive backgrounding, hand the job to the platform — background\_downloader wraps URLSession background transfers and Android's WorkManager.

Treat the payload as untrusted input and make the data layer the only place where a contract change is allowed to fail.

### The three failures and their defences
- A new unknown field must be ignored. Map-based parsing does that for free; the danger is a strict decoder or an assertion over key counts, so do not add one.
- An unknown enum value must fall back, not throw. With json\_serializable, annotate the field with `unknownEnumValue:` and keep an `unknown` member in the enum. Hand-written parsers need the same default in their switch.
- A field turning null must not crash a widget three layers away. Model it as nullable, decide the fallback while mapping to the domain entity, and never use `!` on decoded JSON.

### Rules that make this systematic
- Parse defensively at the boundary: small typed readers that check the runtime type and return a default, instead of a bare `as String` on every key. A number arriving as a string is the most common surprise.
- Convert parse failures into your typed error hierarchy, so a contract break surfaces as a controlled failure and one log line, not as a random exception inside build().
- For lists, decode item by item and skip the bad ones when partial data is better than an empty screen — count and report what you dropped.
- Keep real captured payloads as fixtures in tests. Parsing them is what turns a backend change into a red CI run rather than a production incident.
- Log the failing key path and a redacted snippet of the payload, otherwise you learn nothing from the crash report.
- Be a tolerant reader and a strict writer: accept extra fields, send exactly the documented ones.
- Ask the backend for versioned endpoints for breaking changes; tolerant parsing buys you time, it does not replace versioning.

Dio sets no timeouts at all by default, so a stalled request lives as long as the OS socket lets it.

### What each option covers
- `connectTimeout` — opening the TCP and TLS connection. Fails as `DioExceptionType.connectionTimeout`; 5-10 s is the usual value.
- `sendTimeout` — writing the request body, so a GET with no body never trips it.
- `receiveTimeout` — the wait before the first response byte, and then the gap between byte events. It is not a limit on the whole download: a server trickling one byte a second never trips it.
- `transformTimeout` (dio 5.10+) — bounds the decoding step, which matters when a huge JSON body is being parsed.
- For all of them, `null` or `Duration.zero` means no limit.

### The trap
None of these is a budget for the whole call. Connect, send and receive each get their own clock, so a slow-but-alive request outlives all three. For a hard deadline, wrap the call in `.timeout()` and cancel the `CancelToken` from `onTimeout` — `.timeout` abandons the Future, it does not close the socket, and without the cancel the download keeps running in the background.

### Numbers that hold up on mobile
- Connect 5-10 s, receive 15-30 s for ordinary JSON.
- Long or disabled receive timeout for downloads, uploads and long-lived streams — a per-request `Options` overrides the base values for exactly those calls.
- `package:http` has no timeouts of its own: use `.timeout()` on the call, or `IOClient(HttpClient()..connectionTimeout = ...)`.

Pick the numbers from the UX side. The right limit is the point where the user would rather see an error and a retry button than a spinner.

The term is being interpolated into a URL string, so `#` starts a fragment and `&` starts a new parameter — the server never sees what the user typed.

### What the string version does
- `Uri.parse('https://api.example.com/search?q=$term')` with `term = 'C# & Java'` produces `?q=C` plus a fragment. Everything after the `#` never leaves the device, and the `&` splits the rest into junk parameters.
- Percent-encoding is not optional for `#`, `&`, `+`, `%`, spaces and every non-ASCII character.

### Build the Uri from parts
- `Uri.https('api.example.com', '/search', {'q': term})` encodes each value with `Uri.encodeQueryComponent`, so the space becomes `+` and `#` becomes `%23`.
- With Dio, pass `queryParameters:` instead of writing the query into the path — it encodes values the same way. A `List` value repeats the key (`tag=dart&tag=flutter`); `ListFormat` changes that when the backend wants `tag[]=` or a comma-joined list.
- Never pre-encode a value you hand to either API. `Uri.encodeComponent` plus their own escaping gives you `%2520`, and double encoding is the other half of this bug.

### Path segments are not query parameters
- Dio concatenates `baseUrl` and `path` as plain strings and only normalises the result, so an id containing `/` silently changes the route and a `..` collapses a segment away.
- Escape the segment with `Uri.encodeComponent(id)` when you interpolate, or build the whole Uri with `pathSegments`, which escapes `/` inside a segment as `%2F`.
- The same concatenation means `'https://api.example.com/v1'` plus `'users'` gives `/v1users`. Keep the leading slash on the path.

Rule of thumb: the only string you build by hand is the path template. Every value that came from a user or a server goes in through `queryParameters` or `pathSegments`.

Retry only what is safe to repeat, back off exponentially with jitter, and let the server's `Retry-After` override your own schedule.

### What may be retried
- GET, HEAD, PUT and DELETE are idempotent by contract. POST is not: retry one only when it carries an idempotency key the backend deduplicates on, or a timed-out payment becomes two payments.
- Retry `connectionError`, `connectionTimeout`, `receiveTimeout`, 408, 429, 502, 503 and 504. Never 400, 401, 403, 404 or 422 — the identical request will fail identically.
- Never retry a cancelled request, and stop retrying once the screen that asked is gone.

### The delay
- Exponential and capped: 500 ms, 1 s, 2 s, at most three attempts, plus a ceiling on total time so the UI is not frozen for a minute.
- Add jitter. Without randomisation every device that lost the same cell tower retries in lockstep and hands the recovering server a second outage.
- `Retry-After` on a 429 or 503 is either seconds or an HTTP date. Honour it instead of your own backoff.

### Where it lives
- Dio: one `onError` interceptor that re-sends with `dio.fetch(err.requestOptions)` and keeps the attempt counter in `options.extra`, so a permanent failure cannot loop.
- `package:http`: `RetryClient` from `package:http/retry.dart` — three retries, a 500 ms delay growing 1.5x, and it only retries 503 until you pass `when`.
- Keep it in exactly one layer. A retrying interceptor under a retrying repository under a "Try again" button is eight requests for one tap.

Retries hide a blip; they turn a real outage into a self-inflicted flood. Cap the attempts, cap the total time, then show the error.

Dio already decodes a large JSON body in a background isolate; the jank you are left with is your own `fromJson` mapping running on the UI isolate.

### What Dio does for you
- The default transformer in dio 5 is `FusedTransformer(contentLengthIsolateThreshold: 50 * 1024)`: it fuses the UTF-8 and JSON decoders, and for bodies over 50 KB it runs the decode in an isolate through `compute`.
- It reads the size from `Content-Length`; without that header it buffers the bytes and measures them.
- The fast path applies only to `ResponseType.json` with a JSON content type and no custom `responseDecoder`. Set a custom decoder and you are back on the main isolate.

### What is still yours
- `jsonDecode` hands back `List<Map<String, dynamic>>`. Turning 10,000 of those into models is often the larger half of the cost, and it runs after the transformer has finished.
- Move the whole job: request `ResponseType.plain`, then `Isolate.run(() => parseFeed(raw))` so decoding and mapping happen together and only the models cross back.
- The result is copied back across the isolate boundary. Plain data classes copy cheaply, but measure on the timeline rather than assuming.

### The traps
- `Isolate.run` and `compute` spawn an isolate per call — a few milliseconds and a fresh heap. One call per payload is a win; one per list item is slower than doing nothing.
- `compute` takes a top-level or static function. `Isolate.run` takes a closure, but everything it captures must be sendable: capture `this`, a `BuildContext`, a `Ref` or a live `Dio` and it throws at runtime.
- Flutter web has no isolates. `compute` runs the function inline and `Isolate.run` is unsupported, so on web the only fix is a smaller payload.
- Often the real fix is the API. No amount of off-thread work beats not shipping 3 MB to a screen that shows twenty rows.

All five 401s started their own refresh: the first one rotated the refresh token, and the other four presented a token the server had just revoked.

### Single-flight refresh
- Hold one `Future<String>?` in the interceptor. The first 401 assigns it; every later 401 awaits the same future instead of calling the endpoint again.
- Before refreshing, compare the token the failed request actually sent with the one you hold now. If it already changed, just replay with the new one — no refresh needed.
- Mark the replayed request (`options.extra['retried'] = true`) so a second 401 is rejected instead of looping forever.
- Refresh through a separate `Dio` that has no auth interceptor, or the refresh call re-enters your own interceptor on its first 401.
- `QueuedInterceptorsWrapper` is dio's built-in take on the same idea: it serialises the interceptor so only one request at a time reaches `onError`.

### What "log out" should mean
- Only a 4xx from the refresh endpoint is a real logout. A `connectionError` is not, or a tunnel ride signs the user out.
- Clear the tokens and navigate once, from one place — not from every repository that saw a failure.

### Details that bite in production
- With rotating refresh tokens, persist the new pair inside the single-flight future, before any queued request is replayed.
- Queued requests must take the header at replay time; the `RequestOptions` they were built with still carry the dead token.
- Refresh proactively when you can read `exp` from the JWT. A 30 s skew removes most 401s, and with them most of this queueing.

A new client means a new connection pool, so every call repeats the DNS lookup, the TCP handshake and the TLS handshake instead of reusing a socket that is already open.

### What the pool actually holds
- Dio's `IOHttpClientAdapter` caches one `dart:io` `HttpClient`, and that client owns the keep-alive pool. One long-lived `Dio` is one pool.
- `HttpClient.idleTimeout` defaults to 15 seconds: inside that window a second request to the same host reuses the connection and skips both handshakes, which is 100-300 ms on a mobile network.
- `persistentConnection` is true by default. Set it to false, or throw the client away, and there is nothing to reuse.
- `maxConnectionsPerHost` is unlimited by default — worth capping when a server or a rate limiter dislikes bursts.

### Lifecycle rules
- Build one `Dio` per API (base URL plus its interceptors) at start-up, in whatever holds your dependencies, and inject it.
- `dio.close(force: true)` aborts requests that are in flight, so never close a shared client from a widget's `dispose`. Cancel with a `CancelToken` instead.
- The same rule governs `package:http`: a `Client` created per call gets no reuse, and `close()` kills what is still running.

### When the pool is not enough
- `dart:io`'s `HttpClient` speaks HTTP/1.1 only. For HTTP/2, system proxies, VPN behaviour and platform certificate handling, swap in `native_dio_adapter`, which is backed by cupertino\_http on iOS and cronet\_http on Android.
- If the first screen's latency matters, warm the pool at start-up with one cheap request to the same host.

Clients are infrastructure with a lifetime measured in app sessions. The requests and models are the throwaway part.

Bound how many requests are in flight and collect a per-item outcome, so the pool is never flooded and one failure cannot discard the successes.

### Why `Future.wait` does both wrong things
- The futures are already running before `wait` sees them — building the list starts every request. `wait` only observes.
- With the default `eagerError: false` it waits for all of them and then completes with the first error, dropping every value it had collected; the `cleanUp` callback is the only thing that ever sees those values, and the later errors are discarded silently.
- With `eagerError: true` it throws at the first failure while the other 199 keep running, burning battery and bandwidth for a screen that already shows an error.

### Bounded concurrency
- Run 4-8 at a time: a semaphore built from `Completer`s, `Pool(6).withResource(...)` from `package:pool`, or a worker loop over a shared queue.
- That range is not arbitrary — it is what a rate limiter, the keep-alive pool and a phone radio all tolerate. Past it, latency grows without throughput.
- Give the whole fan-out one `CancelToken` and check it between items, so leaving the screen drains the queue instead of finishing it.

### Keep the partial results
- `futures.wait` — the Dart 3 extension on `Iterable<Future>` — throws a `ParallelWaitError` whose `values` and `errors` are indexed per future, so you can render what arrived and retry only the rest.
- Or map each call to a result type and never throw: a failed item becomes an error tile in the list instead of an empty screen.

The honest interview answer: 200 round trips is a design problem. Ask for a batch endpoint and keep the pool for the cases the backend cannot batch.

`receiveTimeout` measures the gap between byte events, not the length of the response, so a stream that idles between heartbeats trips it — disable it for this request and parse the body line by line instead of chunk by chunk.

### Reading the stream
- Ask for `ResponseType.stream` with `Accept: text/event-stream`; `response.data!.stream` is a `Stream<Uint8List>`.
- Pipe it through `utf8.decoder` and `LineSplitter`. A TCP chunk is not an event: one chunk can hold three events or half of one, and a multi-byte character can be split across two chunks — the decoder handles that, a hand-rolled `String.split` does not.
- The wire format is lines of `data:`, `event:`, `id:` and `retry:`. A blank line dispatches the accumulated event, several `data:` lines join with a newline, and a line starting with `:` is a comment — which is what most servers send as a heartbeat.

### Staying connected
- Set `receiveTimeout: Duration.zero` on this request's `Options`, or a value longer than the server's heartbeat interval, and leave the base value alone for normal calls.
- Remember the last `id:` and send it as `Last-Event-ID` when you reconnect; the server resumes from there. Use the server's `retry:` as the base delay, with backoff and jitter on repeated failures.
- Hold a `CancelToken` and cancel it in `dispose`. A forgotten stream keeps a socket and its subscription alive for the rest of the session.

### When the stream looks frozen
- A proxy or a compressing middlebox can buffer until its own buffer fills. Servers avoid it with `Content-Encoding: identity` and `X-Accel-Buffering: no`; if the client sees nothing for a minute and then everything at once, it is not a client bug.
- On Flutter web use the browser's `EventSource` from `package:web` — it handles reconnect and `Last-Event-ID` for you, but it cannot send an `Authorization` header, so the token has to travel another way.
